extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, and law students (practitioners in patent litigation)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and substantive standards governing wrongs and remedies in patent law, with emphasis on injunctions, contractual relations (assignments/licenses), and jurisdictional allocation between federal and state courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of rights in unpatented invention
rubrics_metrics.description: By the performance of an inventive act the inventor acquires a property in the invention which vests in him by the law of nature; he may retain that property while preserving secrecy, and under American law can use it publicly for a period before applying for a patent without forfeiting exclusive rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The property in an unpatented invention is entitled to the same protection as other property; rights invaded by force or fraud are vindicated by courts and wrongs are redressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of rights in patented invention (scope of monopoly)
rubrics_metrics.description: The issue of a patent confers an exclusive monopoly: the patentee may prohibit others from practising the invention and the monopoly prevails over later independent inventors; the patentee owns the invention as exclusive property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any act impairing commercial importance or converting proceeds of enjoyment gives rise to legal remedy; remedies should be ample and efficient within human jurisprudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of contractual rights of inventors and transferees
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions may be conveyed in interests (assignments) or by license; different relations (assignor/assignee vs licensor/licensee) give rise to distinct rights and obligations which are protected and vindicated according to the nature of the injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses two groups: conveyance transferring monopoly (assignors/assignees, grantors/grantees) and conveyance operating on the invention alone (licensors/licensees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of assignors and assignees (contract consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignor's principal right is to recover the agreed price; assignee's rights include transfer of invention and patent according to contract, recovery of purchase money on total failure of consideration, enforcement of warranties (express and implied), and remedy for fraud or bad faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignee entitled to good faith and fair dealing from assignor; remedies for breach include damages and rescission where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights and remedies of licensors and licensees
rubrics_metrics.description: Licensor entitled to license fees/royalties and to compliance with license restrictions; licensee may repudiate a license and recover fees in some circumstances, is entitled to defense against infringers, and may rely on covenants and estoppel arising from the license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensee's remedies include specific performance, rescission, breach of contract suits, recovery of monies paid; licensor's remedies include rescission, actions for royalties and license fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: General division of wrongs and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject of wrongs and remedies is divided into: I. Wrongs against owners of unpatented inventions; II. Wrongs against patentees; III. Wrongs between contracting parties; remedies are considered in connection with each class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framework for analyzing what law and remedies apply to a given dispute.

rubrics_metrics.name: State vs Federal remedies distinction (preliminary jurisdictional rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some remedies and wrongs are remedied in federal courts, others in state courts; it's necessary to determine whether a wrong invades rights protected by federal or state law to identify the proper forum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction is especially important for rights in patented inventions because some depend on U.S. law (federal) and others on state law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal jurisdiction by diversity of citizenship (non-exclusive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts derive jurisdiction from parties' residence (diversity) as well as subject-matter; where parties are citizens of different states federal jurisdiction exists but is not exclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules determining diversity jurisdiction are common to many wrongs; discussion of subject-matter jurisdiction assumes same citizenship unless otherwise stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal courts' exclusive jurisdiction over cases arising under the Patent Laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdiction grounded on subject-matter has been vested in federal courts over all cases arising under the Patent Laws; this jurisdiction is exclusive — suits arising under Patent Laws cannot be cognizable in local/state courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The line dividing patent cases from others is defined by principle and precedent; exclusivity applies regardless of parties' residence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'cases arising under the Patent Laws' — effect on monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases arising under the Patent Laws are those that affect the monopoly created by the Patent Laws (i.e., the exclusive right conferred by the patent), not mere collateral property or contract rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If controversy does not involve existence/preservation of the monopoly, it's not a case under the Patent Laws and belongs to ordinary tribunals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three classes of controversies that affect the monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: Controversies affecting the monopoly take three forms: (1) dispute over legal existence of the monopoly (patentability); (2) dispute over existence of monopoly in favor of the patentee (title); (3) dispute over the character/scope of matters embraced by the monopoly (scope/claim construction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any controversy fitting one of these forms is a patent law case for federal jurisdictional purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-patent controversies (contract/property) belong to state law
rubrics_metrics.description: Controversies that concern property rights or contractual rights collateral to the monopoly — even if related to patents — are to be determined under general (state) law and do not constitute cases under the Patent Laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include contract disputes that do not require deciding patent validity or scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction: value of preventive equitable action
rubrics_metrics.description: Preventive equitable (injunctive) action has value in cases of expected infringement and can protect patent rights before full trial on the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity aims to afford complete protection where appropriate; injunctions provide preventive relief for prospective injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classes of injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Two main classes: preliminary (temporary) injunctions and perpetual (permanent) injunctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different standards and procedures apply to preliminary versus perpetual injunctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction: discretion of the court guided by established rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Granting a preliminary injunction is a matter of judicial discretion but is guided by established equitable rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court weighs established equitable principles (e.g., balance of harms, adequacy of legal remedy) in exercising discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction: grantable only to prevent prospective injury where no other adequate remedy exists
rubrics_metrics.description: A preliminary injunction should be granted only to prevent prospective (future) injury, and only when there is no adequate remedy at law available to prevent that injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires showing of potential irreparable harm and inadequacy of damages as remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction: grant or refusal not subject to appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: An interlocutory decision to grant or refuse a preliminary injunction is generally not appealable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects equity practice on provisional orders (subject to later review in merits/trial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction: prerequisites — validity, title, and danger of infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A preliminary injunction is properly granted only when the patent is valid, the plaintiff holds title, and there is danger of infringement by the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court evaluates probability of success on the merits (validity & title) and likelihood of imminent infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of validity for preliminary injunction: prior judgment, public acquiescence, admissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof of a patent's validity for injunction purposes can rest on factors such as prior judicial judgments in its favor, public acquiescence, or admissions of the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each form of proof has differing evidentiary weight depending on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior judgments as evidence of validity — circumstances determine weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior judicial determinations may be evidence of validity, but the weight given depends on circumstances (identity of parties, issues, and available testimony).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider identity of parties, identity of issues, and whether the prior judgment was on a full hearing, by consent, or tainted by collusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-judgment subfactors: identity of parties, identity of issues, identity of available testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on a prior judgment as proof of validity, courts consider whether parties are the same, whether the issues litigated were identical, and whether evidence/testimony available then matches current case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of identity on these dimensions reduces the prior judgment's persuasive weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior judgments: treatment of judgments from different tribunals (Supreme/Circuit/Patent Office)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgments from higher courts (Supreme Court), circuit courts, or even patent office proceedings may be considered; their respective weight depends on source and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions of supreme or circuit courts generally carry greater weight; Patent Office proceedings have more limited effect but may still be relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public acquiescence as evidence of validity — definition, weight, and manifestation
rubrics_metrics.description: Public acquiescence (long-continued public non-resistance to a patentee's claim) can be evidence of validity; courts consider how acquiescence is defined, how to measure its weight, and how it is manifested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquiescence requires sufficient publicity and duration to show public recognition of the patent's validity; weight is comparative to prior judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative weight of prior judgments vs public acquiescence
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts compare and balance the evidentiary weight of prior judgments and public acquiescence when assessing validity for injunctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neither is conclusive alone; context and quality of evidence govern which is more persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions of defendant as evidence of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Admissions by the defendant (e.g., acknowledgments of patent scope or ownership) may serve as evidence supporting validity or title for preliminary relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admissions are fact-specific and may be powerful where they exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of plaintiff's title
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff seeking a preliminary injunction must prove title to the patent right asserted (ownership or proper assignment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof may include assignment documents, chain-of-title evidence, and lack of competing claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of intended (or imminent) infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain a preliminary injunction a plaintiff must show evidence of intended or imminent infringement by the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May be shown by defendant's acts, admissions, advertisements, or conduct indicating intent to infringe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may grant injunction on alternative proof or withhold despite proofs presented
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may grant a preliminary injunction on proofs other than those enumerated or may withhold injunction even if typical proofs are presented, depending on equities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes judicial discretion and the equitable balancing of factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for refusal of preliminary injunction — no irreparable injury
rubrics_metrics.description: A primary ground to refuse a preliminary injunction is absence of irreparable injury — if harm can be remedied by damages, injunction is inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court requires showing that legal remedies are inadequate and harm cannot be fully compensated by money.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for refusal — plaintiff's laches or acquiescence
rubrics_metrics.description: If plaintiff has unreasonably delayed (laches) or acquiesced in defendant's conduct, equitable relief may be denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay and prior conduct of patentee are considered in equitable balancing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for refusal — estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Equitable estoppel (e.g., plaintiff's representations inducing defendant reliance) can bar preliminary injunctive relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estoppel requires reliance by defendant and prejudice if injunction issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for refusal — improper purpose by plaintiff
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plaintiff seeks injunction for an improper purpose (e.g., to harass or for competitive advantage beyond patent protection), relief may be denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine motives and the propriety of requesting equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for refusal — defendant's good faith or defendant's patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant's good faith (e.g., independent invention) or existence of defendant's own patent may weigh against granting a preliminary injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court may refuse relief where defendant has a valid competing patent or acted in good-faith belief of non-infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for refusal — doubts as to existence of proper conditions / disastrous consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: If the court has doubts about whether proper equitable conditions exist or if granting would cause disastrous consequences, it may refuse relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable discretion allows consideration of public interest and balance of harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction: granted without reserve if plaintiff is entitled
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plaintiff clearly meets the requirements, a preliminary injunction may be granted without reserve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong showing on merits and equities supports an unqualified injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond and account ordered in lieu of injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may order bond and accounting in lieu of an injunction as an alternative protective measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bond may secure potential damages to defendant; accounting may protect plaintiff's future monetary recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may be enjoined (scope of parties subject to injunction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Injunctions may bind public corporations, private corporations, co-partners, co-owners, assignees, licensees, agents, etc.; courts consider relationships and reach of order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination depends on party's connection to infringing activity and equitable power over them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may be enjoined — defendant ceasing to infringe
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may consider whether the defendant has ceased infringing when deciding whether to issue or maintain an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cessation may affect necessity of continued equitable relief (mootness vs ongoing risk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of application for preliminary injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: There are procedural requirements and forms for applying for a preliminary injunction (petition/bill, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper pleading, supporting affidavits, and evidence must be presented per equity practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice to defendant of application; appearance and answer
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally defendants must be given notice of application for injunction and opportunity to appear and answer, subject to narrow exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where ex parte relief is sought, specific standards and burdens apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions arising on application and hearing: production of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications raise issues to be heard with production of evidence in support and opposition; courts examine factual and legal proofs at the hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate presentation of evidence by both sides informs the equitable decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex parte hearings and burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Ex parte preliminary relief is permitted in limited circumstances; the burden on applicant is high and courts scrutinize urgency and risk of irreparable harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex parte orders are exceptional and often require prompt return hearings with notice to affected parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and scope of injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction must be appropriately tailored in form and scope to the injury and the rights protected, not broader than necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope determined by patent claims, the conduct enjoined, and equitable considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect, dissolution, and enforcement of injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Injunctions have legal effect (obligations on defendant), may be dissolved or modified upon changed circumstances, and violation can lead to contempt and attachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may order attachment for contempt, issue orders of attachment when appropriate, and impose penalties for contempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation of defendant to obey injunction; how and by whom violated
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant is obligated to obey injunctions; courts analyze modes of violation and which actors (agents, licensees, co-owners) may be held in contempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations by third parties acting under defendant's control may also be enjoined or sanctioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application for attachment for contempt and order of attachment: when issued
rubrics_metrics.description: Where injunctions are disobeyed, plaintiff may apply for attachment for contempt; courts issue orders of attachment according to contempt procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards include proof of willful disobedience and consideration of due process protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty for contempt
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts can impose penalties (fines, imprisonment, sequestration of property) for contempt for violating injunctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalties calibrated to coerce compliance and punish willful disobedience within equitable powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetual injunction: when granted
rubrics_metrics.description: A perpetual (final) injunction is granted upon a final determination that the patent is valid, plaintiff entitled, and equitable conditions favor permanent relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final injunctions follow full adjudication on merits; courts may tailor relief or withhold it on equitable grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetual injunction: duration and suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: Perpetual injunctions typically endure for the life of the patent, but courts may suspend, limit, or otherwise condition duration under equitable principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspension or limitation may be used where equitable circumstances or public interest counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetual injunction by consent and dissolution on violation
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may consent to perpetual injunctions; courts also provide for dissolution or modification if terms are violated or circumstances change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consent agreements are enforceable but subject to court approval and equitable oversight.
